# No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?

SII & Xinxu AI

###### Abstract

Pre-training is where every foundation model begins; bringing recursive
self-improvement (RSI) there would let AI improve the process that
creates AI, and could change how the entire industry builds foundation
models. Yet public RSI work has so far targeted only post-training,
which starts from an existing base model, runs trials costing GPU-hours,
and returns verifiable scores. RSI for pre-training breaks all three
conditions at orders-of-magnitude higher cost: a run consumes hundreds
of thousands of GPU-hours over months and cannot be repeated; its
objective, post-training headroom, cannot be read off any single score;
and what must improve is not a model but the whole production &
organization system, from data pipelines and training infrastructure to
the teams that run them. To our knowledge, we are the first in the world
to apply RSI to an entire frontier pre-training run from scratch, and to
report it in detail. RSI does not stop at frontier pre-training, but it
changes form: since no end-to-end loop can close over a single
unrepeatable run, we decompose the _pre-training loop_ into smaller
loops that can, each repairing a step the full run breaks.

The result is 801-30B-A3B-Base,^(†)^(†) We present 801 (pronounced
eight-oh-one), named after the classroom where it was built. a 30B-A3B
MoE model trained from scratch on 11.8T tokens in three months by a
newly formed team. We release it as a _base_ model: full post-training
is left to a subsequent release, and the lightweight SFT reported here
(6B tokens, no RL) only probes post-training headroom. As a base model,
801-30B-A3B outperforms Qwen3-30B-A3B and
Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B, trailing only the larger
Qwen3.5-35B-A3B, and keeps this position under identical SFT; with
lightweight SFT alone, it achieves the highest average on four agentic
benchmarks against fully post-trained models, including Qwen3.6-35B-A3B.
Post-training RSI starts where this work ends: it presupposes a strong
base model, exactly what pre-training must produce. Bringing RSI into
pre-training thus acts on the foundation every later stage builds on. We
will open-source 801-30B-A3B-Base and the lightweight SFT data, a
ready-made resource for evaluating the post-training headroom of base
models, at
[https://github.com/GAIR-NLP/801-30B](https://github.com/GAIR-NLP/801-30B).

## 1 Introduction

Recursive self-improvement (RSI), in which a system turns its own
experience and feedback into persistent changes that improve its
capability, has moved quickly from idea to practice. Agents now run the
loop
$`\textit{propose}\rightarrow\textit{run}\rightarrow\textit{measure}\rightarrow\textit{update}`$
on neural architectures ([Xu et al., 2026b](#bib.bib83)), GPU kernels
([Yu et al., 2026](#bib.bib36); [Fu et al., 2026a](#bib.bib1)), agent
harnesses ([Xia et al., 2026](#bib.bib72)), and, closest to model
building, on post-training itself ([NeoHorse Team et al.,
2026](#bib.bib12); [Rank et al., 2026](#bib.bib96); [Huang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib97)). Where these loops touch pre-training, they do so
through small-scale proxies: data-curation and data-selection strategies
validated on small models ([Mi et al., 2026](#bib.bib85); [Xu et al.,
2026c](#bib.bib84); [Meng et al., 2026](#bib.bib98)), or single-GPU
training runs measured in minutes ([Karpathy, 2026](#bib.bib100); [Guo
et al., 2026](#bib.bib99)). These settings share three conditions: they
start from an existing base model or a toy-scale one, each trial costs
GPU-hours or less, and each returns a verifiable score. Pre-training is
where every foundation model begins, and it satisfies none of the three.
Bringing RSI there would let AI improve the very process that creates
AI; yet, to our knowledge, no public work has attempted it on a full
frontier pre-training run.

RSI for pre-training is not a harder instance of RSI for post-training
but a different regime (Table
[1](#S1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")).
First, it breaks run. A single run consumes hundreds of thousands of
GPU-hours over months, and most projects can afford only one at full
length. An ablation that isolates a single cause costs GPU-weeks, so
most hypotheses are never tested end to end. Second, it breaks measure.
The goal of pre-training is not the highest score today but headroom for
post-training. A run that chases the metric can quietly borrow against
post-training, for example by annealing in supervised fine-tuning (SFT)
data too early, or by collapsing output diversity at the expense of the
headroom that reinforcement learning (RL) later relies on ([Yue et al.,
2025](#bib.bib77)). Such an objective cannot be read off any single
score, and if even a crisply defined benchmark gets overfit by
self-improvement loops ([Xia et al., 2026](#bib.bib72)), a target this
diffuse offers far more ways to be hacked than to be met. Third, what
must improve is not a model but a production system and the organization
that runs it. Before a single token is trained, the data must be built:
in our run, six pipelines with more than 30 processing stages turned raw
web pages, documents, and code into 1,053 data subsets. The training
stack evolved through more than 130 infrastructure code versions and 106
hyperparameter fields. Behind these artifacts stands an organization:
data, infrastructure, training, and evaluation teams, each holding a
different part of the evidence, with the hardest problems falling
between them. A load-balance anomaly, for instance, surfaced in training
metrics but traced to an infrastructure change interacting with
optimizer settings (Section
[3](#S3 "3 Debugging Loops ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?"));
no single team could have closed that loop alone. Improving pre-training
therefore means improving how the organization divides work, shares
evidence, and remembers what it has learned. Post-training RSI starts
where this system ends: it presupposes a strong base model, which is
exactly what the system must produce.

|                    |                                                                   |                                                                                         |
| ------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
|                    | RSI for post-training                                             | RSI for frontier pre-training (ours)                                                    |
| Starting point     | An existing base model                                            | Random initialization                                                                   |
| Cost per trial     | GPU-hours (e.g., 10 H100-hours ([Rank et al., 2026](#bib.bib96))) | Hundreds of thousands of GPU-hours for one run                                          |
| Full-length trials | Tens to hundreds                                                  | One                                                                                     |
| Signal at measure  | Verifiable task score                                             | Post-training headroom, not readable from any single score                              |
| Data               | A fixed dataset or environment                                    | Built from raw sources: 6 pipelines, $`>`$30 stages, 1,053 subsets, 10.5T unique tokens |
| Infrastructure     | A training script                                                 | $`>`$130 code versions, 106 hyperparameter fields                                       |
| What improves      | A model or a harness                                              | A production system and the organization that runs it                                   |
| Who is in the loop | One agent or researcher                                           | Data, infrastructure, training, and evaluation teams with their agents                  |

Table 1: RSI for Post-training vs. RSI for frontier pre-training operate
in different regimes.

Small-scale proxies and scaling laws seem to offer a fast loop, but a
cheap loop cannot answer every expensive question. Seemingly minor
fitting choices shift the fitted exponent ([Besiroglu et al.,
2024](#bib.bib11); [Weng, 2026](#bib.bib71)), small differences at
fitting scale grow large at trillion-token scale, and a ladder of proxy
runs assumes that scale is the only thing changing ([Weng,
2026](#bib.bib71)). Once a question couples architecture, recipe,
infrastructure, and multi-source data mixtures, the proxy study needed
to settle it becomes as expensive as the run it was meant to de-risk. We
therefore use our two pilot runs to surface and eliminate problems, not
to extrapolate scores.

If the end-to-end loop cannot be rerun, where do agents earn their
place? The run leaves behind a vast context: internal metrics,
hyperparameter changes, data-mixture edits, infrastructure diffs, and
dozens of evaluations on every intermediate checkpoint, far more than
any team can read, let alone remember. The characteristic waste in this
regime is not a bad experiment but re-investigating a question settled
weeks earlier, because no one linked the symptom to its class of cause.
The bottleneck thus shifts from compute to institutional memory: what
was tried, what failed and why, and which signals co-occurred. Agents
earn their place by recalling and attributing across evidence no human
will finish reading, and, wherever a fast signal can be built, by doing
the work itself: building data-pipeline components, crawling the web,
and generating agentic training data at a breadth no team could manage
by hand.

Our answer to the question in the title is that RSI does not stop at
frontier pre-training, but it changes form. Since no end-to-end loop can
close over a single unrepeatable run, we decompose pre-training into
smaller loops that can close, each repairing a step the full run breaks.
_Debugging loops_ relocate run onto the infrastructure and data stacks,
which can be rerun cheaply; the _headroom loop_ repairs measure for the
run as a whole; and _experience-to-metric loops_ build a measure where
none existed. A shared _context infrastructure_ serves as the
organization’s memory: it integrates evidence across teams and preserves
negative results and their reasons, which is where the update step
persists and the recursion lives (Figure
[2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")).

Figure 2: The standard RSI loop
($`\textit{propose}\rightarrow\textit{run}\rightarrow\textit{measure}\rightarrow\textit{update}`$)
does not close in frontier pre-training: a run takes months and cannot
be repeated, and today’s score does not reflect the headroom a
checkpoint leaves for post-training. We propose three types of loops,
instantiated as six practical loops. Debugging loops comprise the infra
debugging loop and the data debugging loop, which trace internal-metric
and output anomalies to their causes. The headroom loop is instantiated
as the recipe loop, using headroom measurements to guide the whole
pre-training process. Experience-to-metric loops comprise the classifier
development loop, the site discovery loop, and the crawl-coverage loop,
turning experience-based judgment into measurable feedback. All six
loops share a context infrastructure that integrates evidence across
teams at scale.

We built these loops while training 801-30B-A3B, a 30B-A3B
Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) ([Shazeer et al., 2017](#bib.bib63)) model
trained from scratch on 11.8T tokens in three months by a newly formed
team. To our knowledge, this is the first public account of RSI applied
to an entire frontier pre-training run. Our contributions are:

- •
  _(a) Debugging loops (Section
  [3](#S3 "3 Debugging Loops ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?"))._
  An _infra debugging loop_ and a _data debugging loop_, driven by
  internal-metric and output anomalies, respectively. Across two pilots
  (stopped at 1T and 3T tokens) and the main run, agents localized
  causes spanning infrastructure, data, and recipe, from a load-balance
  penalty interacting with optimizer state to low-diversity synthetic
  data, and resolved five cross-stack diagnoses in about one month.
  Together with data and recipe revisions, these fixes raised the mean
  score over 22 benchmarks (Appendix
  [B](#A2 "Appendix B Benchmarks for Pre-training Monitoring ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?"))
  at a matched 1T-token budget from 47.78 (initial pilot) to 51.96
  (revised pilot) to 56.83 (main run).
- •
  _(b) A headroom loop (Section
  [4](#S4 "4 Headroom Loop ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?"))._
  Because base scores do not preserve post-training rankings, we judge
  checkpoints by what they are _worth_ after adaptation, using tiny-SFT,
  a learning aptitude curve, and a max-over-protocols estimate of the
  capability ceiling. These measurements separate apparent stagnation in
  base evaluation from continued gains after adaptation.
- •
  _(c) Experience-to-metric loops (Section
  [5](#S5 "5 Experience-to-Metric Loops ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?"))._
  Classifier development, site discovery, and crawl coverage, in which
  agents turn judgment once made by feel into recorded, quantitatively
  evaluated workflows. We built six data pipelines from scratch this
  way.
- •
  _(d) Agentic data at pre-training scale (Section
  [6](#S6 "6 Scaling Agentic Data into Pre-Training ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?"))._
  Agents cross from consuming training to producing it: 220K executable
  pull requests rolled out across nine harnesses yielded more than 100B
  tokens of verified agentic trajectories (134B agentic tokens in
  total), used in the long-context stage of pre-training.

##### What we release and how to compare it.

We release 801-30B-A3B-Base as a _base_ model. Full post-training is
left to a subsequent release; the lightweight SFT reported here (6B
tokens, no RL) serves only to probe post-training headroom. We therefore
compare at three levels, from the fairest to the least favorable to us
(Section
[8](#S8 "8 Evaluation ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")).
(1) _Base against base_: 801-30B-A3B outperforms Qwen3-30B-A3B ([Yang et
al., 2025a](#bib.bib75)) and Nemotron-3.5-Lightning-30B-A3B ([NVIDIA et
al., 2026](#bib.bib46)), trailing only the larger Qwen3.5-35B-A3B ([Qwen
Team, 2026a](#bib.bib59)). (2) _Identical SFT_: when every base model is
fine-tuned on the same SFT data, it keeps this position. (3)
_Lightweight SFT against full post-training_: even so, it achieves the
highest average across four agentic benchmarks among the fully
post-trained models we compare, including Qwen3.6-35B-A3B ([Qwen Team,
2026b](#bib.bib60)). The third comparison pits a few billion SFT tokens
against complete vendor post-training pipelines; we report it as a
reference point for headroom, not as a like-for-like comparison. We will
open-source 801-30B-A3B-Base and the lightweight SFT data, a ready-made
resource for evaluating the post-training headroom of base models, at
[https://github.com/GAIR-NLP/801-30B](https://github.com/GAIR-NLP/801-30B).

## 2 Adapting RSI to Frontier Pre-Training

Recursive self-improvement (RSI) is the idea that a system turns its own
experience and feedback into persistent changes that improve its
capability and, in the strongest form, the process of improvement
itself. The engine behind it is a closed loop, exemplified by
AlphaEvolve ([Novikov et al., 2025](#bib.bib44)) and ASI-Evolve ([Xu et
al., 2026c](#bib.bib84)). We write that loop as
$`\textit{propose}\rightarrow\textit{run}\rightarrow\textit{measure}\rightarrow\textit{update}`$
and use it as the operational definition of RSI throughout this report.
In this report, the improving system is the pre-training project itself,
comprising its agents, researchers, and infrastructure, rather than the
model being trained.

The four steps are worth defining precisely. _Propose_ forms a candidate
change or hypothesis, the role played by the generator in
generate-critique-revise schemes ([Madaan et al., 2023](#bib.bib41)) and
by the proposer in proposer-solver self-play ([Zhao et al.,
2025](#bib.bib78)). _Run_ realizes that candidate to produce evidence,
by training, rolling out, or executing it. _Measure_ scores the evidence
against a signal that stands in for human judgment or the desired
target. [Chen et al. (2026)](#bib.bib15) arrange candidate signals into
a verification hierarchy, from formal verifiers at the strong end to a
model’s intrinsic self-assessment at the weak end. _Update_ folds the
outcome back into a persistent change, keeping what scored higher and
discarding the rest, and in the recursive case it also revises the loop
machinery that produced the change. This persistence is what makes the
loop recursive rather than a one-off search.

Two preconditions decide whether this loop improves anything. The first
is cheap, repeatable iteration: gains compound only when a trial is
cheap enough that run and update can cycle many times. The second is a
reliable signal at measure, aligned with the true goal. Without an
external signal there is no reliable improvement ; with a weak or
misaligned one, the loop degenerates through self-confirming errors,
model and diversity collapse ([Shumailov et al., 2024](#bib.bib64)), or
frame lock-in on a well-posed but wrong objective ([Chen et al.,
2026](#bib.bib15)).

As argued in Section
[1](#S1 "1 Introduction ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?"),
frontier pre-training breaks both preconditions: a full-length run
cannot be repeated, and its true objective, post-training headroom, is
too diffuse to serve as a trustworthy measure. The system that must
improve is, moreover, an organization rather than a model. The standard
end-to-end loop therefore does not transfer to this regime. We keep the
loop, but change where it closes.

|                      |                                                                |                                                                     |                                                       |                                            |
| -------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------ |
| Loop type            | Propose                                                        | Run                                                                 | Measure                                               | Update                                     |
| Debugging            | A suspected cause: code version, configuration, or data subset | Targeted diagnosis on the infra or data stack; cheap and repeatable | Does the anomaly disappear?                           | Apply the fix; record ruled-out causes     |
| Headroom             | A recipe change, or whether to continue training               | Pilots and main-run checkpoints; costly and not repeatable          | Tiny-SFT, learning aptitude, max-over-protocols       | Revise the recipe; judge training progress |
| Experience-to-metric | A new prompt, model, or crawler version                        | Component-level evaluation; cheap                                   | Task-specific evaluation set; SEO page-count estimate | Deploy, or iterate again                   |

Table 2: How each loop type instantiates the four RSI steps. Debugging
and experience-to-metric loops close quickly on cheap components; the
headroom loop closes only a few times per project, because its run is
the pre-training run itself.

![Refer to caption](2611.10719v1/figures/model-metric.png)

Figure 3: Overview of internal training metrics and external evaluation
protocols for pre-training monitoring.

##### Three types of loops.

Rather than casting pre-training as one score-driven loop, we close
three types of smaller loops around it, with six concrete instances
(Figure
[2](#S1.F2 "Figure 2 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")).
Table
[2](#S2.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 2 Adapting RSI to Frontier Pre-Training ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")
shows how each type instantiates the four steps.

- •
  _Debugging loops_ relocate run onto the infrastructure and
  data-pipeline stacks, where a diagnosis can be rerun cheaply. They are
  driven by anomalies rather than by a score to maximize: measure asks
  whether the anomaly disappears, and each ruled-out cause is recorded
  as a negative result. The _infra debugging loop_ traces unusual
  internal metrics to infrastructure code or training-recipe settings,
  and the _data debugging loop_ traces unusual output patterns to a
  specific data source or processing stage (Section
  [3](#S3 "3 Debugging Loops ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")).
- •
  The _headroom loop_ repairs measure for the run as a whole. Its signal
  is post-training headroom, estimated through tiny-SFT, learning
  aptitude, and max-over-protocols evaluation rather than read off a
  base-model score. It is instantiated as the _recipe loop_, which uses
  these measurements to revise the recipe from the two pilots, stopped
  at 1T and 3T tokens, to main pre-training, and to monitor progress
  within the main run (Section
  [4](#S4 "4 Headroom Loop ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")).
  Because its run is the costly run itself, it closes only a few times
  per project.
- •
  _Experience-to-metric loops_ build a measure where none existed. Steps
  such as building data-pipeline components and acquiring web data were
  historically tuned by hand; we give each an explicit evaluation, such
  as a task-specific evaluation set or an SEO page-count estimate, so
  that revisions can be compared. This type is instantiated as the
  _classifier development loop_, the _site discovery loop_, and the
  _crawl-coverage loop_ (Section
  [5](#S5 "5 Experience-to-Metric Loops ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")).

##### Context infrastructure.

These loops operate on different parts of pre-training, but all require
evidence that spans teams: an anomaly may connect a model’s output to a
data-processing decision made weeks earlier, headroom measurements must
be read alongside recipes and checkpoint histories, and data workflows
must retain the evaluations behind each revision. We built a _context
infrastructure_ to integrate this evidence (internal metrics such as
per-layer loss, per-module gradient norms, and expert load-balance
statistics, together with hyperparameter changes, data-mixture edits,
infrastructure diffs, and checkpoint evaluations), produced by agents
and by researchers who separately own the data, infrastructure,
training, and evaluation stacks, at a scale no team can read unaided
(Table
[1](#S1.T1 "Table 1 ‣ 1 Introduction ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")).
It records not only what was tried but what failed and why, so that
negative results become persistent knowledge. This is where the update
step persists and where the recursion in our loops lives: each new
proposal starts from what earlier iterations have ruled out, and agents
direct their effort to the next unresolved bottleneck instead of
rediscovering old ones.

##### From pilots to main pre-training.

Together, these loops supported revisions of the data and training
recipe across two pilots and main pre-training (Figure
[4](#S2.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ From pilots to main pre-training. ‣ 2 Adapting RSI to Frontier Pre-Training ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")).
The initial pilot stopped at 1T tokens, the revised pilot at 3T, and the
main run used approximately 11.8T tokens; the figure shows main
pre-training through Stage1-1 at 7T. These revisions brought together
debugging, headroom assessment, and quantitatively evaluated data
workflows.

At 1T tokens the mean score over the 22 common benchmarks rises from
47.78 to 51.96 to 56.83, and at 3T tokens main pre-training reaches
59.94 against the revised pilot’s 56.48. Because data and recipe changed
together, these gains reflect the combined iterations supported by the
three types of loops rather than any single fix. The following sections
describe how each type contributed to this process.

Figure 4: Two pilots and the main pre-training in a three-month period.
_Top_: main configuration changes; matching colors link each iteration
to its evaluation curves below. _Bottom_: initial pilot (warm brown) and
revised pilot (gray-blue) stopped at 1T and 3T tokens, respectively;
main pre-training (dark teal) is shown through Stage1-1 at 7T tokens.
The five subset scores are means over their constituent benchmarks, and
Overall is the mean over all shared benchmarks.

## 3 Debugging Loops

This section shows the two debugging loops operating on the context
infrastructure as we introduced in Section
[2](#S2 "2 Adapting RSI to Frontier Pre-Training ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?").
(1) The _infra debugging loop_ traces unusual internal metrics to
infrastructure code or training-recipe settings. (2) The _data debugging
loop_ traces unusual output patterns to a specific data source or
processing stage (Figure
[5](#S3.F5 "Figure 5 ‣ 3 Debugging Loops ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?");
Table
[2](#S2.T2 "Table 2 ‣ 2 Adapting RSI to Frontier Pre-Training ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")
maps both loops to the four RSI steps). Unlike conventional RSI
approaches, which improve performance by repeatedly training and
comparing candidate models, these loops operate within a single
pre-training run. Rather than restarting training to evaluate new
candidate models, they continuously identify, attribute, and eliminate
problems as training progresses, improving the ongoing run itself. We
conclude with the five cross-stack diagnoses produced by these loops
(Table
[3](#S3.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 3.3 Accumulated Diagnoses ‣ 3 Debugging Loops ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")).

Figure 5: The debugging loops are instantiated as (a) the infra
debugging loop and (b) the data debugging loop.

### 3.1 Infra Debugging Loop

The infra debugging loop uses internal training metrics as the starting
point for identifying and resolving anomalies during pre-training. By
linking these signals to infrastructure code and training-recipe
configurations through the context infrastructure, agents can trace
unexpected model behavior to its underlying causes, propose targeted
fixes, and verify their effects within the ongoing training run. We
illustrate this process through the anomalies observed in the two pilot
runs, following four steps: detect, attribute, fix, and verify.

Detect. During the two pilot runs, agents scanning internal metrics
through the context infrastructure identified two contrasting patterns
in MoE load-balancing indicators (Figure
[6](#S3.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 3.1 Infra Debugging Loop ‣ 3 Debugging Loops ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")).
In the initial pilot, both aggregate and layer-wise MaxVio ([Wang et
al., 2024a](#bib.bib67)) declined to low levels under a strong balancing
penalty, raising concerns about potential over-balancing. The revised
pilot revealed a different pattern: layers 15 and 18 developed large,
persistent MaxVio violations, while the aggregate remained within a
typical range. This discrepancy showed that aggregate monitoring alone
could obscure severe layer-specific imbalance. Layer 48, the final
layer, was also elevated, but we do not treat this alone as evidence of
failure, since its function is closely tied to the output space.
Together, these two patterns illustrate why monitoring MoE load
balancing requires examining both aggregate trends and layer-specific
deviations.

Attribute. To identify the source of these anomalies, agents used the
context infrastructure to correlate metric trajectories with
infrastructure code commits and optimizer configurations. By searching
across more than 130 infrastructure code versions and 106 hyperparameter
fields, they narrowed the cause to a change in the load-balance penalty
implementation and its interaction with optimizer state updates for
certain parameter groups. This process established an attribution chain
from training stagnation to internal-metric anomalies, and from those
anomalies to specific infrastructure and configuration changes. Rather
than treating unusual metrics as isolated symptoms, agents traced them
across the training stack to identify their underlying causes.

Fix. Based on this diagnosis, we first revised the pilot configuration
by lowering the load-balancing ([Fedus et al., 2022](#bib.bib25))
coefficient from $`10^{-2}`$ to $`10^{-4}`$, reducing the learning rate
from $`2.7\times 10^{-3}`$ to $`5\times 10^{-4}`$, and switching the
optimizer for router parameters from Muon ([Jordan et al.,
2024](#bib.bib34); [Liu et al., 2025](#bib.bib39)) to AdamW ([Loshchilov
and Hutter, 2019](#bib.bib40)). These settings were carried into main
pre-training, with two further adjustments: computing the load-balance
loss over the global batch rather than per micro-batch ([Qiu et al.,
2025](#bib.bib57)), and excluding normalization and bias parameters from
weight decay. Because several factors changed together, the comparison
does not isolate the contribution of any single adjustment. Together,
these changes constituted the revised training configuration used in
main pre-training.

Figure 7: Layer-wise load imbalance rises as downstream evaluation gains
diminish during training. The gray shaded region marks the same interval
(approximately 2.2–6T tokens) in both panels. (a) Layer-15 MaxVio

Verify. Subsequent training shows that the revised configuration
mitigates layer-wise load imbalance and suggests that internal metrics
may reveal potential training problems earlier than downstream
evaluation alone. (1) First, the revised configuration substantially
mitigated the layer-specific imbalance observed in the pilot. At a
matched training budget of 3T tokens, layer-15 MaxVio had already
exceeded 14 in the revised pilot, whereas it was around 5 in main
pre-training, with pronounced escalation occurring only at a later stage
(Figure
[7](#S3.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 3.1 Infra Debugging Loop ‣ 3 Debugging Loops ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")).
This indicates that the revised configuration substantially alleviated
the earlier anomaly, although it did not eliminate it entirely. (2)
Second, the internal metrics provided a more granular view of training
dynamics than downstream evaluation alone. During main pre-training,
layer-15 MaxVio rose sharply over approximately 2.2–6T tokens (the
shaded interval in Figure
[7](#S3.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 3.1 Infra Debugging Loop ‣ 3 Debugging Loops ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")).
Over the same interval, downstream evaluation gains gradually
diminished. After approximately 6T tokens, layer-15 MaxVio remained at a
high plateau, while downstream evaluation gains within Stage1-1 had
largely flattened. This temporal correspondence suggests a possible
association between layer-wise load imbalance and training saturation.
Layer-wise MaxVio rises well before downstream performance plateaus,
indicating that internal metrics can flag potential training problems
while evaluation scores are still improving. Monitoring these metrics
alongside downstream evaluations may therefore enable earlier
investigation and intervention.

Finally, the context infrastructure allows these diagnostic experiences
to persist across iterations. Because the previous diagnosis and its
supporting evidence were preserved, the recurrence of similar anomalies
could be anticipated rather than rediscovered from scratch. This allowed
us to use the early MaxVio signal as a basis for further investigation,
rather than waiting until downstream evaluation gains had flattened.

### 3.2 Data Debugging Loop

Figure 8: Diagnosing bad patterns in model outputs. _Top_: three
representative output patterns, a credential leak with a
verbatim-repeated config block, a jump into a fixed “Does this sentence
make sense?” QA template, and a self-spawning chain of near-identical
word problems. _Bottom_: the eight-step loop that traces each pattern
back to a data-pipeline defect. Agents handle detection, tracing, and
inspection at scale, humans set triage priority and approve the fix.

During the two pilots, we continuously monitored the output behavior of
the trained model. Agents identified recurring patterns in the model’s
responses to greetings and common questions, which are indicative of
repetitive, low-diversity, or insufficiently cleaned training data. They
extracted these anomalous patterns and searched the data pipeline for
matching signatures at scale.

Anomalous patterns. Figure
[8](#S3.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 3.2 Data Debugging Loop ‣ 3 Debugging Loops ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")
illustrates three representative patterns observed in model outputs. (1)
First, _credential leakage and repetition_: given the prompt deepseek,
the model emits a secret resembling an API key, followed by repeated
copies of an identical proxy-configuration block, continuing until the
generation length limit is reached. (2) Second, _jumping to a fixed QA
template_: when given a natural request for a dinner recommendation, the
model fails to answer the question and instead switches to a fixed “Does
this sentence make sense?” multiple-choice template, proceeding to solve
this invented task. (3) Third, _self-spawning repetitions_: given only
the marker \*\*New Example:\*\*, the model generates an unbounded
sequence of nearly identical division word problems, each following the
same four-step solution scaffold.

Automated diagnosis process. The bottom of Figure
[8](#S3.F8 "Figure 8 ‣ 3.2 Data Debugging Loop ‣ 3 Debugging Loops ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")
illustrates how agents trace these anomalous patterns back to specific
data-pipeline defects. The eight-step process can be organized into
three stages. (1) The first stage is _detection and pattern extraction_.
Agents identify anomalies in model-generated samples or evaluation
results and classify the corresponding cases. Based on the identified
patterns, agents write detectors and perform large-scale matching across
all 1,053 data subsets to identify those potentially containing the
corresponding anomalies. (2) The second stage is _attribution and
localization_. After candidate data subsets have been identified, humans
determine the priority of investigation. Agents then trace these subsets
to their data pipelines (six in total) and inspect the intermediate data
produced at more than 30 processing stages across these pipelines,
ultimately locating the specific data sources and processing stages
responsible for the anomalies. (3) The final stage is _resolution and
verification_. Once the source of an anomaly has been identified, agents
propose fixes to the data or pipeline. Humans decide whether to approve
their execution. Approved fixes are applied to the relevant processing
stages, followed by model re-evaluation to verify their effectiveness;
rejected proposals are returned for revision.

Throughout this process, agents handle large-scale anomaly detection,
data tracing, and stage-by-stage inspection, while humans retain control
over two key decision points: investigation prioritization and fix
approval. This division of labor makes large-scale investigations
systematic and practical, beyond what could reasonably be accomplished
through manual inspection alone.

Root cause attribution and fixes. Through this process, the three
anomalous patterns were traced to three distinct data-pipeline defects.
(1) First, the credential-leakage and repetition case was traced to
insufficiently cleaned configuration files in the code corpus. These
files contained sensitive information and repetitive configuration
content that had entered the training data and subsequently surfaced in
model generations. We addressed this issue by fixing the corresponding
data-processing stage to remove such inadequately cleaned content. (2)
Second, the fixed-QA-template case was traced to insufficient filtering
of synthetic data in a subset of an open-source QA corpus. This subset
contained a large volume of “Does this sentence make sense?” questions.
We strengthened synthetic-data filtering at the corresponding stage to
reduce the presence of such fixed-template examples in the training
data. (3) Finally, the self-spawning case was traced to a synthetic-data
pipeline whose prompt design lacked sufficient diversity, resulting in
highly similar generated examples. We revised the corresponding prompt
design to improve the diversity of the synthetic data. For all three
cases, we modified the corresponding data-pipeline stages and
re-evaluated the model after applying the fixes to verify their
effectiveness.

### 3.3 Accumulated Diagnoses

The two debugging loops described above illustrate how agents identify
anomalies in model behavior and trace them back to underlying issues in
the infrastructure, training recipe, and data pipeline. However, these
are only representative examples of a broader effort to diagnose and
resolve problems throughout the training process.

Across the two pilots and main pre-training, we applied the same
approach to systematically investigate issues across different parts of
the training system. Many of these issues could not be attributed to a
single component. Diagnosing them required connecting evidence from
internal metrics, infrastructure code, training configurations, and data
pipelines, and tracing the interactions among them. Table
[3](#S3.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 3.3 Accumulated Diagnoses ‣ 3 Debugging Loops ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")
summarizes five cross-stack issues identified and resolved through this
process, covering load balancing, optimizer configurations, data
quality, weight decay, and data loading. These findings demonstrate how
agents, supported by the context infrastructure, can identify and
resolve problems that span multiple parts of the training system.

|                |                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                   |                                                                                                                                                                                                               |
| -------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Area           | Finding                                                                                                                                                                                                                                           | Fix                                                                                                                                                                                                           |
| Load balancing | Expert load was either over-balanced across all layers or severely imbalanced in a few individual layers (Figure [6](#S3.F6 "Figure 6 ‣ 3.1 Infra Debugging Loop ‣ 3 Debugging Loops ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")). | Adopt global-batch load balancing ([Qiu et al., 2025](#bib.bib57)), which relaxes the per-micro-batch constraint and allows experts to specialize.                                                            |
| Optimizer      | Weight-norm and gradient-norm trends diverged across modules.                                                                                                                                                                                     | Reassign which modules use Muon and which stay on AdamW (Table [5](#S7.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 7.2 Optimizer Allocation ‣ 7 Training Recipe of 801-30B-A3B ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")). |
| Data quality   | Pilot models generated advertisements, which were traced to advertisements and low-quality web pages remaining in the training corpus.                                                                                                            | Filter them further with quality classifiers.                                                                                                                                                                 |
| Weight decay   | Router logits showed abnormal trends during training.                                                                                                                                                                                             | Exclude normalization and bias parameters from weight decay.                                                                                                                                                  |
| Data loader    | When resuming a training task with the same global batch size but a different DP size, the sampler did not preserve the per-step data order of the previous task.                                                                                 | Restore the per-step sample order of the previous task when resuming with a different DP size.                                                                                                                |

Table 3: The five cross-stack diagnoses resolved with the context
infrastructure across the two pilots and main pre-training.

Beyond the fixes themselves, the time required to complete these
diagnoses demonstrates the value of the context infrastructure. In our
experience, diagnosing issues of this kind can take months without such
infrastructure. With the support of agents and the ability to connect
evidence across the training stack, we completed all five diagnoses in
roughly one month, substantially reducing the manual effort required to
identify and trace the problems.

More importantly, the value of these diagnoses extends beyond the
immediate fixes. The context infrastructure preserves the observations,
attempted fixes, and negative results from each investigation, allowing
subsequent iterations to build on previous findings rather than start
from scratch. Each investigation thus contributes not only to improving
the ongoing training run, but also to a growing body of knowledge that
can be reused in future iterations. Together, the two debugging loops
turn individual problem-solving efforts into a cumulative process of
continuous improvement, with concrete data and training-recipe
improvements carried forward into the successive iterations shown in
Figure
[4](#S2.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ From pilots to main pre-training. ‣ 2 Adapting RSI to Frontier Pre-Training ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?").

## 4 Headroom Loop

The goal of pre-training is not to maximize today’s score but to leave
the greatest headroom for post-training. Measuring this headroom can
supply the signal for the headroom loop. We first describe three
complementary measurements (Section
[4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Measuring Post-Training Headroom ‣ 4 Headroom Loop ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")),
then show what they revealed that base evaluation did not (Section
[4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Measuring Post-Training Headroom ‣ 4 Headroom Loop ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")),
and finally how the recipe loop used them (Section
[4.2](#S4.SS2 "4.2 The Recipe Loop ‣ 4 Headroom Loop ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")).

### 4.1 Measuring Post-Training Headroom

We use three measures to assess post-training headroom: Tiny-SFT,
learning aptitude, and max-over-protocols evaluation. Together, they
capture three aspects of a model’s potential: its performance after
limited post-training, its efficiency in learning from additional data,
and the capabilities it can demonstrate under evaluation protocols.

Figure 9: Tiny-SFT data composition and validation. _Left:_ Token
composition of the 6.33B-token mix. Math, Science ([Xu et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib3)), and Code ([Ahmad et al., 2025](#bib.bib2)) each
contribute approximately 2.00B tokens (31.6%), while instruction
following ([Pyatkin et al., 2025](#bib.bib56)) contributes 0.331B tokens
(5.2%). _Right:_ Qwen3-30B-A3B versus its base model
(Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base) after one epoch of Tiny-SFT. Scores are percentages
across 13 benchmarks; the fine-tuned model scores higher on 10 of them.
This validation supports the effectiveness of Tiny-SFT as a proxy for
monitoring model performance after limited post-training.

Figure 10: Apparent stagnation in base evaluation can coexist with
improving post-SFT performance. (a) Direct base-model Overall_Avg over
pre-training; red boxes mark the checkpoint intervals examined in (b)
and (c). Each point in (b) and (c) reports SFT AVG13 after applying the
same SFT procedure independently to a checkpoint from (a). (b) Stage1-1,
steps 123,000–210,000 (4.1T-7T tokens): post-SFT scores improve by 1.49
points despite the near-flat base trend. (c) Stage1-3, steps
243,000–345,000 (8.1T-11.5T tokens): post-SFT scores improve by 2.39
points while base scores fluctuate around a plateau.

Tiny-SFT. Base-model evaluation alone does not fully capture a model’s
potential after post-training. We therefore apply a small SFT budget to
each evaluated pre-training checkpoint and directly measure its
performance on benchmarks designed for post-trained models. The
resulting scores approximate how the checkpoint would perform after a
representative post-training phase, providing a more realistic measure
of its downstream potential. The SFT corpus spans multiple task
categories to approximate the diversity of actual post-training
workflows (Figure
[9](#S4.F9 "Figure 9 ‣ 4.1 Measuring Post-Training Headroom ‣ 4 Headroom Loop ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")).
We note that SFT was not repeated with multiple random seeds, so small
differences between adjacent checkpoints should be interpreted with
caution. In our experiments, Tiny-SFT helped us identify two interesting
patterns that are not readily apparent from base-model evaluation alone:

Figure 11: Base and post-SFT checkpoint rankings are not
interchangeable. _Left_: base Overall_Avg and SFT AVG13 for the same
checkpoints. _Right_: all paired checkpoints, sorted by base rank within
each group, with their corresponding SFT ranks. Rank 1 is best, ties
receive average ranks, and $`\rho`$ denotes Spearman correlation
computed within each group from the reported scores. Base and SFT scores
use different benchmark suites.

> (1) False stagnation. We observed that base-model scores can appear to
> plateau, even as the model continues to improve after SFT. Figure
> [10](#S4.F10 "Figure 10 ‣ 4.1 Measuring Post-Training Headroom ‣ 4 Headroom Loop ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")
> shows two intervals in which average base-model scores fluctuate
> around a near-plateau, while average scores after SFT continue to
> improve. In Stage1-1, from step 123,000 to 210,000 (4.1T–7T tokens),
> the average base-model score remains near 61, while the average score
> after two epochs of SFT increases from 65.34 to 66.83. In Stage1-3,
> from step 243,000 to 345,000 (8.1T–11.5T tokens), the average
> base-model score stays around 64–66, while the average score after one
> epoch of SFT rises from 70.54 to 72.93. It is worth noting that the
> base-model and post-SFT scores are computed over different benchmark
> collections. We therefore compare their trends within each evaluation
> setting rather than their absolute values. These results show that
> relying only on base-model evaluation could lead to premature
> decisions to stop training or unnecessary changes to the training
> recipe.
>
> (2) Ranking disagreement. We also found that the relative ranking of
> checkpoints can change after SFT, compared with their ranking under
> base-model evaluation. To examine this difference, we paired 23
> pre-training checkpoints with their available SFT results and compared
> their average base-model scores across the 22 public and internal
> benchmarks listed in Appendix
> [B](#A2 "Appendix B Benchmarks for Pre-training Monitoring ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")
> with their average scores after SFT (Figure
> [11](#S4.F11 "Figure 11 ‣ 4.1 Measuring Post-Training Headroom ‣ 4 Headroom Loop ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")).
> Since checkpoints early in training have weaker instruction-following
> ability, we used the same Tiny-SFT data but assigned different SFT
> budgets across training stages. Specifically, we computed rankings
> separately for 13 Stage1-1 checkpoints evaluated after two SFT epochs
> and 10 Stage1-2/Stage1-3 checkpoints evaluated after one epoch. The
> corresponding Spearman rank correlations are 0.796 and 0.438. The
> rankings are positively associated, particularly in Stage1-1, but they
> do not provide the same assessment of checkpoint headroom. For
> example, within the Stage1-1 group, step 159,000 ranks first under
> base-model evaluation but third after SFT, whereas step 210,000 moves
> from sixth to first. Between these checkpoints, the average base-model
> score decreases from 61.41 to 60.76, while the average score after SFT
> increases from 66.22 to 66.83. These results show that base-model
> scores alone cannot fully capture differences in post-training
> potential across checkpoints.

Figure 12: A toy illustration of learning aptitude. Thin lines with
hollow markers are raw scores at SFT checkpoints, and each straight line
is their least-squares fit of Eq.
([1](#S4.E1 "In 4.1 Measuring Post-Training Headroom ‣ 4 Headroom Loop ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")):
the intercept $`b`$ is the score at the first checkpoint $`N_{0}`$, and
the slope $`k`$ is the gain per tenfold increase in post-training data.
The model with high learning aptitude starts lowest, yet reaches the
target score $`s^{*}`$ with about $`15\times`$ less data than the
baseline (Eq.
([2](#S4.E2 "In 4.1 Measuring Post-Training Headroom ‣ 4 Headroom Loop ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?"))).
The high-start, flat model only reaches it at the end of the plotted
budget.

Learning aptitude. A model’s initial performance does not necessarily
reflect how effectively it can learn from additional post-training data.
We therefore measure its _learning aptitude_, which captures how
efficiently a model improves as the post-training data budget increases.

To measure learning aptitude, we select a specific domain or task family
and fine-tune different base models using the same domain-specific SFT
data. We evaluate a sequence of intermediate checkpoints throughout
training to track how each model’s performance changes as it sees more
data. This allows us to fit a learning curve and measure how efficiently
the model learns from additional data. For most models, scores grow
approximately linearly with the logarithm of the post-training data
budget. We therefore fit a log-linear learning curve for each base model
$`m`$ (Figure
[12](#S4.F12 "Figure 12 ‣ 4.1 Measuring Post-Training Headroom ‣ 4 Headroom Loop ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")):

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       s_{m}(N)=b_{m}+k_{m}\log_{10}\frac{N}{N_{0}},
       ```                                            |     | (1) |

where $`s_{m}(N)`$ is the downstream score after $`N`$ units of
post-training data (in practice, SFT steps at a fixed batch size), and
$`N_{0}`$ is the data budget of the first evaluated SFT checkpoint. The
intercept $`b_{m}`$ is the score at this first checkpoint, representing
the model’s initial performance in the domain. The slope $`k_{m}`$
measures the score gain for every tenfold increase in post-training
data, capturing how efficiently the model learns from additional data.
We estimate both parameters by ordinary least squares over all SFT
checkpoints, excluding the untuned base model.

Neither parameter alone captures a model’s learning aptitude. A model
with a high initial score but a shallow learning curve starts strong but
gains little from additional data. In contrast, a model with a lower
initial score but a steeper learning curve may eventually surpass it as
the data budget increases. We therefore consider both parameters
together and estimate the amount of post-training data required for
model $`m`$ to reach a target score $`s^{*}`$:

|     |     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
|     |

       ``` math
       N_{m}^{*}(s^{*})=N_{0}\cdot 10^{(s^{*}-b_{m})/k_{m}},
       ```                                                    |     | (2) |

We then compare this data requirement with that of a baseline model,
using the ratio $`N^{*}_{\text{base}}/N^{*}_{m}`$ to measure data
savings. A larger ratio means that the model requires less post-training
data to reach the same target performance.

In this work, we use learning aptitude to compare different models
rather than different checkpoints within a single training run. As shown
in Section
[8](#S8 "8 Evaluation ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?"),
a model with a lower initial score but higher learning aptitude can
eventually surpass a model with a higher initial score after sufficient
fine-tuning. Applying this measure to checkpoint selection within a
single training run is a natural direction for future work.

Max-over-protocols evaluation. A model’s evaluation score does not
always fully reflect its acquired capabilities, as the extent to which
these capabilities are demonstrated can depend on the evaluation
protocol. The same benchmark may yield very different scores under
perplexity scoring, few-shot prompting, and zero-shot prompting (Figure
[13(a)](#S4.F13.sf1 "In Figure 13 ‣ 4.1 Measuring Post-Training Headroom ‣ 4 Headroom Loop ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?");
protocol definitions in Appendix
[C](#A3 "Appendix C Evaluation Protocols for Base Models ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")).
Moreover, the relative performance of these protocols can change across
pre-training checkpoints, as illustrated by HumanEval in Figure
[13(b)](#S4.F13.sf2 "In Figure 13 ‣ 4.1 Measuring Post-Training Headroom ‣ 4 Headroom Loop ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?").

A single evaluation protocol may therefore underestimate model’s
capability. To obtain a more complete picture, we evaluate each
checkpoint under all available protocols and take the highest score for
each benchmark. Our goal is to measure the capabilities a model can
demonstrate, rather than how well it adapts to a particular evaluation
format. Taking the maximum across protocols provides a more complete
estimate of the model’s capability ceiling. For cross-model comparisons
in Section
[8](#S8 "8 Evaluation ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?"),
we follow the evaluation protocols specified in that section.

(a) 801-30B-A3B Base scores across benchmarks under different evaluation
protocols. The same benchmark can yield different scores depending on
the protocol, showing that a single evaluation setting may not capture
the capabilities a model has acquired.

(b) HumanEval scores throughout pre-training under different evaluation
protocols. Both the scores and the relative ranking of protocols change
across checkpoints. We therefore take the pointwise maximum across
available protocols at each checkpoint to obtain a more complete measure
of the model’s demonstrated capability.

Figure 13: Assessing base-model capabilities with max-over-protocols
evaluation.

### 4.2 The Recipe Loop

The _recipe loop_ brings post-training headroom measurements into the
pre-training process, using them as feedback to assess training
progress, guide recipe adjustments, and inform subsequent iterations.
The two pilots, stopped at 1T and 3T tokens, and the subsequent main
pre-training run form the sequence of iterations in this loop (Figure
[4](#S2.F4 "Figure 4 ‣ From pilots to main pre-training. ‣ 2 Adapting RSI to Frontier Pre-Training ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")).

Throughout this process, we use headroom measurements to track how the
model’s post-training potential evolves across training stages and feed
the results back into the pre-training recipe. Rather than focusing
solely on current base-model scores, we consider post-training
performance, learning efficiency, and the capabilities the model can
demonstrate under different evaluation protocols. This helps us judge
whether pre-training is still accumulating useful capabilities and
whether the current recipe needs further adjustment.

Based on the issues identified through earlier debugging, we continue to
refine the infrastructure and training configurations while developing
the training data. In particular, main pre-training introduced new QA
data and revised the proportions and sampling weights of web, code,
mathematics, books, and papers.

The central idea is that pre-training progress should not be judged
solely by current base-model scores, but also by whether the model
continues to accumulate capabilities that can be further developed
through post-training. Even when base-model evaluation appears to
plateau, pre-training may still be making meaningful progress if
post-training headroom continues to grow.

## 5 Experience-to-Metric Loops

Many data-processing decisions in pre-training have traditionally relied
on expert experience, such as how to clean and filter data, and how to
judge whether a processing strategy works well. We turn these
experience-driven tasks into standardized workflows with explicit
evaluation metrics. This allows agents to analyze errors, revise their
approaches, compare alternatives, and improve their performance through
repeated iterations.

We call this the _Experience-to-Metric Loop_, and apply it to three
tasks: classifier development, site discovery, and crawl-coverage
optimization. All three follow the same principle: turn human experience
into measurable tasks, let agents carry out and improve the work, and
use evaluation results to guide the next iteration.

### 5.1 Classifier Development Loop

Figure 14: Iterative development of a data classifier. _Left_: a human
defines the classification task (1); a strong model samples data and
annotates an evaluation set (2); an agent analyzes cases and tunes the
labeling prompt (3); the strong model uses that prompt to label training
data (4); a compact classifier is distilled from these labels (5) and
evaluated (6). The component can be deployed as a tuned prompt (Option
A) or a distilled model (Option B). _Right_: accuracy and F1 over three
iterations (v1–v3) for classifiers of ad intent, computing subject, and
clinical health subject.

Earlier work on _Data Darwinism_ provides a framework for the first
question. It introduces a ten-level taxonomy (L0–L9) that organizes data
processing operations, from data acquisition and format normalization to
filtering, model-driven refinement, and synthesis ([Qin et al.,
2026a](#bib.bib86)). Following its use in daVinci-LLM ([Qin et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib87)), we use this framework to guide pipeline design. For
example, OCR belongs to format normalization (L1), rule-based and
model-based filtering correspond to L2–L3, and refinement for cleaning
or repairing content falls under L4. This taxonomy helps us define what
each component should do before choosing its model, prompt, or
implementation.

DataEvolve explores a complementary question: how data-curation
strategies can improve through repeated evaluation and diagnostic
feedback ([Mi et al., 2026](#bib.bib85)). Inspired by this approach, we
develop classifiers, filters, OCR models, and rewriters through a shared
evaluation workflow.Data Darwinism guides the choice of processing
operations, while the evaluation loop helps determine whether a
particular implementation performs its intended task well. Figure
[14](#S5.F14 "Figure 14 ‣ 5.1 Classifier Development Loop ‣ 5 Experience-to-Metric Loops ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")
illustrates this process for classifiers, with three stages (six steps
in the figure).

_Step 1: Define the task and construct an evaluation set._ A researcher
specifies what the classifier should do. A strong model then annotates
representative samples to create a reference evaluation set. This
establishes quality criteria and provides a common basis for comparing
prompts, models, and processing rules. Since the reference labels come
from a strong model, the evaluation measures agreement with that model
rather than with human judgment.

_Step 2: Analyze errors and improve the component._ Agents analyze
hundreds to thousands of examples in parallel, identify recurring error
patterns, and use these findings to revise prompts, compare models, or
adjust processing rules. Each revision is evaluated against the same
task definition and evaluation set, allowing us to determine whether the
changes actually improve performance.

_Step 3: Validate and deploy._ The revised component is evaluated before
deployment. For a classifier, the result can be used as a tuned labeling
prompt or distilled into a smaller model using training data labeled by
the strong model. The distilled classifier is evaluated and the loop
continues revisions improve its performance. The evaluation catches
regressions: in Figure
[14](#S5.F14 "Figure 14 ‣ 5.1 Classifier Development Loop ‣ 5 Experience-to-Metric Loops ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?"),
all three classifiers lost accuracy at v2 before improving at v3.

In under three months, we built six data pipelines, with agents
contributing 36 model-selection decisions as well as prompt optimization
and classifier construction.

### 5.2 Web Acquisition: Site Discovery and Crawl-Coverage Loops

Figure 15: Structure-aware web data acquisition. A human requirement
seeds an agent-driven pipeline with two loops. Loop 1 (site discovery)
expands and verifies related sites through the web’s link structure.
Loop 2 (crawl coverage) crawls each confirmed site to a coverage target
informed by its SEO page estimate. Links, search indexes, and robots
directives are treated as structured signals rather than discarded.

The public web is a major source of pre-training data, but
systematically finding high-quality sources and collecting their content
as completely as possible remain challenging. A common approach starts
from seed documents, uses a classifier to retrieve relevant pages, and
identifies the domains where these pages are concentrated ([Shao et al.,
2024](#bib.bib18)). However, two questions remain: how can we
continuously discover more valuable sites, and how can we tell whether
we have collected enough data from each site?

We address these questions with two connected agent-driven loops: the
_site discovery loop_, which finds high-quality data sources, and the
_crawl-coverage loop_, which aims to collect their content as completely
as possible. Both use information from search-engine-optimization (SEO)
tools, which provide related-site information and estimates of indexed
page counts, as signals to guide discovery and measure crawl coverage.
Figure
[15](#S5.F15 "Figure 15 ‣ 5.2 Web Acquisition: Site Discovery and Crawl-Coverage Loops ‣ 5 Experience-to-Metric Loops ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")
shows the pipeline.

Loop1: Site Discovery Loop. The goal of site discovery is to expand a
small set of high-quality seed sites into a broader collection of
relevant data sources. We use SEO tools to identify candidate sites
related to the seeds through the web’s link structure. An agent then
visits each candidate to check its relevance and quality, adding
verified sites to the seed set for the next round of discovery. We
measure the effectiveness of each round by its _verified yield_, the
number of discovered sites that pass verification. Each round’s verified
sites become seeds for the next round, allowing discovery to expand
iteratively. The process stops when a round produces no new qualified
sites. This turns the experience-based decision of where to look next
into a measurable and repeatable discovery process.

Loop2: Crawl-Coverage Loop. Once valuable sites have been identified,
the next task is to collect their content as completely as possible. For
each confirmed site, an agent writes and runs a crawler, then compares
the number of retrieved pages with the page-count estimate provided by
SEO tools. We use the _coverage ratio_ as the evaluation metric, defined
as the number of retrieved pages divided by the estimated total number
of pages:

|     |     |     |
| --- | --- | --- |
|     |

````math
\text{Coverage Ratio}=\frac{\text{Retrieved Pages}}{\text{Estimated Pages}}
``` |  |

Although SEO page counts are estimates, they provide a quantitative
reference for assessing crawl coverage. The agent compares the retrieved
count with this estimate, investigates potential gaps, revises the
crawler, and runs it again to measure the resulting coverage. In this
way, crawling becomes an iterative process driven by measurable coverage
rather than an informal judgment of when a site is sufficiently crawled.

##### Closing the loops.

The site discovery and crawl-coverage loops address two complementary
challenges in web data acquisition: where to find more valuable data
sources and how to collect their content as completely as possible.
Together with the classifier development loop, they follow the same
principle: turn experience-driven tasks into workflows with explicit
evaluation metrics, so that agents can execute the work, assess the
results, and improve their approaches through repeated iterations.
Specifically, classifier development uses task-specific evaluation
scores, site discovery uses the verified yield of each round, and web
crawling uses the coverage ratio. The key is to give tasks that once
relied on expert judgment explicit objectives and evaluation procedures.
Agents can then use feedback to determine how well a task has been
completed and what to improve next. This turns experience-based
decisions into systematic and repeatable processes, making pre-training
more scientific one component at a time.

## 6 Scaling Agentic Data into Pre-Training

Agentic data, consisting of trajectories generated by agents solving
real-world tasks with verifiable outcomes, has proven effective in
post-training ([Pan et al., 2025](#bib.bib54); [Yang et al.,
2025b](#bib.bib76)). Real-world software development provides a rich
source of such tasks and offers a new opportunity for pre-training. Our
goal is to scale this data source to hundreds of billions of tokens
while preserving task diversity and data quality.

However, achieving this scale requires more than conventional
data-processing pipelines. Real-world software tasks are diverse and
involve complex task construction, execution environments, testing, and
integration across agent harnesses. We argue that *extensive use of
agents is a necessary condition for scaling agentic data into
pre-training*. The main bottleneck is not generating a handful of
high-quality examples, but systematically transforming diverse
real-world software development activities into executable, verifiable,
and scalable training data.

Figure 16: Overview of agentic-data pipeline. The key component is the
Validation gates, which admits a task only when it clears policy,
execution, and semantic checks and the same evaluation fails on the
initial code but passes on the reference, and sanitization into a
Docker/OCI image that keeps the external eval but strips the reference
patch and original history. Rejected tasks return with evidence and fix
hints (dashed path).

### 6.1 Why Agentic Data Requires Agents

Complex task construction and validation. Real software development
offers a rich source of tasks for agentic data. Recent work has explored
several directions: making development tasks executable through
automated environment and evaluation-script construction ([Fu et al.,
2026b](#bib.bib88)), preserving development context and execution
feedback in mid-training trajectories ([Zeng et al., 2026](#bib.bib4)),
and connecting related PRs into longer task chains ([Jiang et al.,
2026](#bib.bib89)).

Scaling this data source to pre-training requires handling the full
diversity of real-world development activity. This includes both PRs
with clear task definitions and well-maintained tests ([Jimenez et al.,
2024](#bib.bib33); [Pan et al., 2025](#bib.bib54); [Badertdinov et al.,
2025](#bib.bib9)), and those with incomplete descriptions, implicit
requirements, or multiple work items bundled together. For each PR, the
pipeline must construct three mutually consistent components: a
reproducible execution environment, an instruction specifying what the
agent is expected to do, and tests and evaluation scripts that verify
whether the task requirements are met.

These components must be developed together. For example, a repository’s
CI may inject environment variables that were omitted from the
constructed environment, causing the evaluation to fail for reasons
unrelated to the code change. In another case, a test may require a
function with a specific name, while the instruction describes only the
desired behavior, causing a valid implementation to be rejected. A
single PR may also bundle multiple work items, leaving the instruction,
environment, and tests with inconsistent task boundaries.

Task construction therefore involves more than simply extracting a task
description from a PR. The environment, instruction, and evaluation must
agree on what the task requires. Agents need to inspect repository
context, identify inconsistencies across these components, and revise
them accordingly. At scale, this process must handle the long tail of
repository-specific conventions and development practices.

![Refer to caption](2611.10719v1/multi_harnesses.png)

Figure 17: The multi-harness rollout layer. A single launch(harness,
prompt, infer_cfg) call in the unified adapter drives all nine
integrated harnesses, which among them speak three API protocols
(Anthropic Messages ([Anthropic, 2026](#bib.bib6)), OpenAI Responses
([OpenAI, 2026b](#bib.bib50)), and OpenAI Chat Completions ([OpenAI,
2026a](#bib.bib49))). The Bifrost gateway ([Maxim AI, 2025](#bib.bib42))
normalizes the three protocols onto one LLM serving backend and injects
inference settings (context length, maximum output, temperature)
centrally.

Multi-harness integration and maintenance. Even after constructing a
task, generating diverse trajectories at scale requires supporting
multiple harnesses during execution. We integrated nine harnesses into
our agentic data pipeline: Claude Code ([Anthropic, 2025](#bib.bib5)),
Codex ([OpenAI, 2025](#bib.bib48)), Pi-Agent ([Earendil Works,
2025](#bib.bib55)), OpenCode ([Anomaly, 2025](#bib.bib52)), OpenHands
([Wang et al., 2025](#bib.bib70)), Droid ([Factory AI,
2025](#bib.bib24)), Hermes ([Nous Research, 2025](#bib.bib43)), OpenClaw
([OpenClaw contributors, 2026](#bib.bib51)), and SWE-agent ([Yang et
al., 2024](#bib.bib74)). Each harness has its own interfaces,
dependencies, and failure modes. Even the same model can behave
differently across harnesses. In addition, harness updates and new
plugins introduce further configuration changes.

As a result, the combinations of models, harnesses, and versions require
ongoing integration and maintenance. We use a unified adapter to launch
rollouts across different harnesses, with agents helping diagnose
execution failures, revise integrations, and validate updated
configurations. As these combinations grow and change, manual
maintenance becomes unsustainable. Agents are therefore necessary for
sustaining large-scale trajectory generation.

|  |  |
|----|----|
|  Category |  Specific behavior |
|  Pull the reference fix from version control |  Fetch its own merged PR diff or the fixing commit patch |
|  |  Recover the fix from unreachable Git objects (git fsck, cat-file) |
|  Fetch upstream code over the network |  Download files from raw.githubusercontent, the GitHub API, or PyPI JSON |
|  |  Clone, fetch, or add a remote pointing at the upstream repository |
|  Install an already-fixed version |  pip download or install --target with a pinned version range |
|  |  Pull packages through conda, apt, or an external mirror (aliyun, tuna, ustc) |
|  Find a solved copy already on disk |  Read installed, cached, or site-packages source copies |
|  |  Scan from root with find, grep, or rg, or walk the conda tree |
|  Tamper with the evaluation |  Write or rewrite test files |
|  |  Deselect or skip the failing tests (pytest --deselect) |
|  Reason then exfiltrate |  Plan in chain-of-thought to leave the sandbox, then issue a network call |

Table 4: Agentic anti-hack patterns, grouped by category. Each is a
concrete way a model can pass a synthesized task without solving it.
Agents scan trajectories for these behaviors and flag candidates for
review or re-synthesis.

Trajectory quality control and anti-hacking. Anti-hacking is critical to
producing high-quality agentic data. Models can exploit evaluation
shortcuts in many ways ([Zhong et al., 2025](#bib.bib80); [jacobkahn,
2025](#bib.bib35)), and agents are essential for detecting such behavior
at scale. In a data synthesis pipeline, agents must distinguish between
two types of problems: *hacks*, where a model bypasses the task rather
than genuinely solving it, and *synthesis defects*, where the execution
environment, tests, or task instructions themselves are flawed. This
distinction is particularly difficult because a model’s cheating
behavior can mask defects in the task, making an invalid task appear
solvable. To address this, agents scan execution trajectories for
anomalous behaviors, such as accessing Git repositories and logs,
downloading related packages, searching for code commits, or using shell
commands that bypass the actual task logic. Suspicious cases are flagged
for human review or re-synthesis (Table
[4](#S6.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 6.1 Why Agentic Data Requires Agents ‣ 6 Scaling Agentic Data into Pre-Training ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")).

Thus, producing agentic data at scale requires not only making tasks
executable, but also verifying that models genuinely solve them and that
the resulting trajectories are trustworthy.

### 6.2 Scaling Agentic Data for Pre-Training

Through the task-construction, multi-harness execution, and
quality-control processes described above, we established a pipeline for
producing agentic data at scale.

Figure 18: Funnel chart of agentic data pipeline. 260K raw PRs are
filtered into 220K executable tasks. Rolling each task out under 9
harnesses gives about 2M trajectories. After verification, 1.1M
trajectories remain, totaling more than 100B training tokens (about 91K
tokens per trajectory on average). Tasks and trajectories are drawn on
separate scales.

More than 84% of the raw pull requests we collected were successfully
converted into executable tasks. For these PRs, we constructed execution
environments, extracted task requirements, and synthesized corresponding
tests (Figure
[18](#S6.F18 "Figure 18 ‣ 6.2 Scaling Agentic Data for Pre-Training ‣ 6 Scaling Agentic Data into Pre-Training ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")).
We then rolled out the resulting 220K executable PRs across nine
harnesses. The trajectories were generated using small and medium-sized
open-weight models, including DeepSeek-Flash and GPT-OSS. After layered
filtering, we obtained 1.1M agent trajectories that met our pre-training
quality standards, totaling more than 100B tokens, with approximately
91K tokens per trajectory on average. Together with trajectories from
other diverse sources, the total volume of agentic data available for
pre-training reached 134B tokens. Importantly, these trajectories are
not merely an auxiliary ingredient for post-training, but a *first-class
data source for pre-training*.

Agent-driven data pipelines represent a shift in how training data is
produced. As models become more capable, they can solve harder tasks and
generate richer training signals. At the same time, as harnesses and
tools evolve, agents can adapt the underlying integration layer. Beyond
adding more harnesses, the plugin ecosystems within each harness are
also growing rapidly, further expanding the space of configurations that
must be supported.

We expect agent-driven data pipelines to become an increasingly
important source of high-quality, diverse, and verifiable training data
for future frontier pre-training runs.
