````math
We adopt the Qwen3-30B-A3B ([Yang et al., 2025a](#bib.bib75))
Mixture-of-Experts architecture, with approximately 30 billion total
parameters and 3 billion active parameters per token. Figure
[21(a)](#S7.F21.sf1 "In Figure 21 ‣ 7 Training Recipe of 801-30B-A3B ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")
summarizes the selected training recipe: three pre-training sub-stages
followed by two context-extension stages. All stages use a global batch
of 33,554,432 tokens and Muon ([Jordan et al., 2024](#bib.bib34); [Liu
et al., 2025](#bib.bib39)), with AdamW ([Loshchilov and Hutter,
2019](#bib.bib40)) for the excluded parameter groups, including
embeddings, the output head, normalization parameters, biases, and
routers.

Stage1 maintains a sequence length of 4,096 tokens. Stage1-1 trains from
scratch through step 210,000 (approximately 7T tokens); Stage1-2
continues to step 240,000 (approximately 8T), and Stage1-3 supplies the
checkpoint at step 345,000 (approximately 11.5T ). At these transitions,
the data mixture is updated and the RoPE ([Su et al., 2024](#bib.bib65))
base increases from $`10^{4}`$ to $`5\times 10^{5}`$ and
$`5\times 10^{6}`$, following the base-frequency adjustment for longer
contexts ([Xiong et al., 2024](#bib.bib73)). The learning rate remains
$`5\times 10^{-4}`$ after an 2,000-step warmup; Stage1-2 and Stage1-3
resume the optimizer and training state without a warmup. Stage1 uses
global-batch load balancing ([Fedus et al., 2022](#bib.bib25); [Qiu et
al., 2025](#bib.bib57)) with coefficient $`10^{-4}`$ and router z-loss
([Zoph et al., 2022](#bib.bib82)) with coefficient $`10^{-3}`$.

Stage2 extends the sequence length to 32,768 tokens and is configured
for 3,000 steps (approximately 100B tokens). Stage3 further extends it
to 262,144 tokens and is configured for 6,000 steps (approximately 200B
tokens). Both retain the RoPE base of $`5\times 10^{6}`$, initialize
from the preceding stage’s weights with fresh optimizer state, use a
1,000-step warmup, and disable both load-balancing and router z-loss
penalties. Stage2 keeps the learning rate at $`5\times 10^{-4}`$ after
warmup, whereas Stage3 applies cosine decay to $`5\times 10^{-5}`$.
Stage3 also enables length-aware packing. The three stages together
correspond to approximately 11.8T tokens.

The training corpus draws from multiple data types (shown in Figure
[20](#S7.F20 "Figure 20 ‣ 7 Training Recipe of 801-30B-A3B ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")):
web text, PDF documents, question-answer pairs, code repositories, and
agentic trajectories. Beyond the agentic data pipeline detailed in
Section
[6](#S6 "6 Scaling Agentic Data into Pre-Training ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?"),
each major category branches into sub-pipelines (shown in Figure
[19](#S7.F19 "Figure 19 ‣ 7 Training Recipe of 801-30B-A3B ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")).
*Web data* is cross-classified by advertisement presence, content type
tags, domain category, and language, creating a Cartesian product of
fine-grained cells that serve as the atomic units for review and mixture
tuning. *Math data* undergoes model-driven rewriting to increase
diversity and refine equation and symbols. *PDF data* passes through OCR
extraction, vision-language model (VLM) refinement to correct OCR
errors, and multi-stage quality filters. *QA data* pipelines classify
whether the problem’s context is complete or not and rollout the CoT
with monitoring pass rate to probe their difficulty. *Code data*
includes static code files and pull-request records.

Figure
[21(b)](#S7.F21.sf2 "In Figure 21 ‣ 7 Training Recipe of 801-30B-A3B ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")
shows how the configured sampling mixture changes across training
stages. These proportions describe sampling weights, whereas Figure
[20](#S7.F20 "Figure 20 ‣ 7 Training Recipe of 801-30B-A3B ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")
reports unique corpus tokens. Stage1-1 assigns 48% to web text and 20%
to code. In Stage1-2 and Stage1-3, the web share falls to 23%, while
papers, books, and QA increase to 20%, 17%, and 10%, respectively. These
two sub-stages share the same category-level proportions, although their
underlying data sources differ. Stage2 removes the dedicated web
component, raises QA to 32%, and assigns 10% to capability-targeted
data. Stage3 introduces a 15% agentic component and assigns 11% to
capability-targeted data, including instruction-following and
long-context examples. The capability-targeted category also includes
retrieved web, book, and paper material, so the absence of a dedicated
web component does not imply the absence of all web-derived content.

### 7.1 Attention-Balanced Data Sampling

Mixing long sequences into training data can cause throughput
degradation far beyond what their proportion would suggest. In theory,
the expected training time should be the proportion-weighted sum of the
time spent on long and short samples. In practice, adding only 10% long
samples can halve the training speed.

Using the context infrastructure, the agent traces this unexpected
slowdown to computation bubbles caused by imbalanced attention workloads
across data-parallel (DP) ranks. In synchronous data-parallel training,
ranks with heavier attention workloads become stragglers, leaving other
ranks idle at synchronization points. This imbalance is particularly
severe for packed sequences, where attention cost depends on individual
document lengths rather than total token count. We estimate each pack’s
cost as where $`m_{p}`$ counts document segments and $`\ell_{p,j}`$ is
the length of segment $`j`$.

|     |                                                  |     |     |
|-----|--------------------------------------------------|-----|-----|
|     |
       ``` math
       \widehat{C}(p)=\sum_{j=1}^{m_{p}}\ell_{p,j}^{2},
       ```                                               |     | (3) |

To mitigate this imbalance, the dataloader sort packs by estimated
attention cost within a bounded window and group similarly costly packs
into global microbatches. When each DP rank receives multiple packs, we
further assign packs in descending cost order to the least-loaded rank
with remaining capacity (Figure
[22](#S7.F22 "Figure 22 ‣ 7.1 Attention-Balanced Data Sampling ‣ 7 Training Recipe of 801-30B-A3B ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")a).

The sorting window limits sample reordering. Larger windows improve load
balance (Figure
[22](#S7.F22 "Figure 22 ‣ 7.1 Attention-Balanced Data Sampling ‣ 7 Training Recipe of 801-30B-A3B ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")b),
but document length may be associated with data source and difficulty.
Aggressive sorting can therefore bias the per-step mixture and
substantially increase loss fluctuations early in long-context training.
We used a limited sorting window with a buffer of roughly twice the
distributed world size to balance computational efficiency and sample
diversity.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 22: (a) Grouping packs by attention cost reduces imbalance;
values are illustrative. (b) Imbalance in our 256K corpus across sorting
windows, using 128 DP ranks and one pack per rank. The ratio is maximum
to mean rank cost, averaged across microbatches; 1 denotes perfect
balance.

![](data:image/svg+xml;base64,)

Figure 23: Training loss with and without attention-balanced data
sampling (32-step moving average).

To evaluate this strategy, we compared two 256K-context pretraining runs
on 256 GPUs with matching configurations. We evaluate the proposed
dataloader on 256 GPUs with context parallelism of 4 (CP=4), yielding 64
data-parallel (DP) replicas. With one pack per DP replica and a sorting
window of eight global microbatches, our method achieves a
$`2.26\times`$ throughput improvement (from 1,126 to 2,543 TGS).
Smoothed training losses follow similar trajectories (Figure
[23](#S7.F23 "Figure 23 ‣ 7.1 Attention-Balanced Data Sampling ‣ 7 Training Recipe of 801-30B-A3B ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")).
Because this scheduling alters the global sample order, we evaluated
final model quality separately, and benchmark differences with and
without scheduling remained within run-to-run fluctuations.

### 7.2 Optimizer Allocation

We use Muon for expert and attention weight matrices, and AdamW for
router, embedding, output, normalization, and bias parameters. To
examine this allocation alongside the optimizer diagnosis in Table
[3](#S3.T3 "Table 3 ‣ 3.3 Accumulated Diagnoses ‣ 3 Debugging Loops ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?"),

[5](#S7.T5 "Table 5 ‣ 7.2 Optimizer Allocation ‣ 7 Training Recipe of 801-30B-A3B ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")).
Three use global load balancing and vary the parameters assigned to
Muon; a fourth uses the same expert-and-attention allocation with local
load balancing. All four use the same configured data mixture, a
sequence length of 4,096, a global batch of 8,192 sequences (33.55M
tokens), and a learning rate of $`5\times 10^{-4}`$ after 2,000 warmup
steps. The load-balancing and router z-loss coefficients are $`10^{-4}`$
and $`10^{-3}`$, respectively.

Figure
[24](#S7.F24 "Figure 24 ‣ 7.2 Optimizer Allocation ‣ 7 Training Recipe of 801-30B-A3B ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")
compares these runs over their evaluation interval, ending at step
18,000 (604B tokens). Under global load balancing, both hybrid
configurations have higher downstream scores than all-AdamW at every
evaluated checkpoint. At the endpoint, Overall_Avg is 45.60 for
all-AdamW, 47.89 for Muon on experts, and 48.28 for Muon on experts and
attention. Their mean LM losses over the last 100 steps are 1.768,
1.746, and 1.737, respectively. Extending Muon to attention provides an
improvement in these runs, although the score gap narrows with training.
The local and global expert-and-attention variants remain close: their
endpoint scores are 48.52 and 48.28. These observations support the
hybrid parameter allocation. Downstream evaluation, however, does not
distinguish local from global load balancing over this interval. We
nonetheless adopt global load balancing for main pre-training because
its internal metrics are more stable. Each setting is represented by a
single training run.

## 8 Evaluation

We evaluate 801-30B-A3B through complementary comparisons of base-model
performance, general capabilities after supervised fine-tuning (SFT),
and agentic capabilities against post-trained models. The base-model
comparison assesses the pre-trained checkpoint directly, while the
Base+SFT comparison examines general capabilities after adaptation. The
agentic comparison further evaluates performance on SWE-bench Verified,
SWE-bench Pro, CyberGym, and KernelBench. These settings are presented
separately to distinguish direct base-model evaluation from downstream
performance after adaptation.

Given current resource and time constraints, we have focused our initial
evaluation and optimization on the settings reported in this section,
with particular emphasis on agentic tasks. We plan to broaden task
coverage and provide more comprehensive evaluation support in future
work.

### 8.1 Evaluation Settings

#### 8.1.1 Base Evaluation Settings

We evaluate base checkpoints on 13 benchmarks across five categories:
commonsense, with ARC-Easy and ARC-Challenge ([Clark et al.,
2018](#bib.bib16)); reasoning, with MMLU-Pro ([Wang et al.,
2024b](#bib.bib68)), MMLU-Redux ([Gema et al., 2025](#bib.bib26)), BBH
([Suzgun et al., 2023](#bib.bib66)), and AGIEval-EN ([Zhong et al.,
2024](#bib.bib79)); code generation, with HumanEval ([Chen et al.,
2021](#bib.bib14)), EvalPlus ([Liu et al., 2023](#bib.bib23)), and
MultiPL-E ([Cassano et al., 2023](#bib.bib13)); mathematics, with GSM-8K
([Cobbe et al., 2021](#bib.bib17)) and MATH-500 ([Lightman et al.,
2024](#bib.bib38)); and science, with GPQA-Main ([Rein et al.,
2024](#bib.bib62)) and SuperGPQA ([M-A-P Team et al.,
2025](#bib.bib22)). Table
[6](#S8.T6 "Table 6 ‣ Prompting and generation. ‣ 8.1.1 Base Evaluation Settings ‣ 8.1 Evaluation Settings ‣ 8 Evaluation ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")
summarizes the default prompting, scoring, and generation settings for
each benchmark. The model-specific protocol-selection procedure is
described at the end of this subsection.

##### Prompting and generation.

All benchmarks use zero-shot prompting except BBH, which uses three
demonstrations, and AGIEval-EN, which uses five. For the non-code
benchmarks, we use greedy decoding with temperature 0 and generate one
candidate per problem. For HumanEval, EvalPlus, and MultiPL-E, we sample
four candidates per problem with temperature 0.2 and top-$`p`$ 0.95.
Each code-generation candidate is limited to 2,048 generated tokens. The
other generation limits range from 1,024 to 16,384 tokens, as listed in
the table.

|  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|----|
| Category | Benchmark | Metric | Shots | Decoding | $`T`$ | Top-$`p`$ | Candidates | Max. tokens |
| Commonsense | ARC-Easy | Exact match | 0 | Greedy |  |  | 1 | 16,384 |
|  | ARC-Challenge | Exact match | 0 | Greedy |  |  | 1 | 16,384 |
| Reasoning | MMLU-Pro | Exact match | 0 | Greedy |  |  | 1 | 16,384 |
|  | MMLU-Redux | Exact match | 0 | Greedy |  |  | 1 | 4,096 |
|  | BBH | Exact match | 3 | Greedy |  |  | 1 | 1,024 |
|  | AGIEval-EN | Exact match | 5 | Greedy |  |  | 1 | 2,048 |
| Code | HumanEval | Avg@4 | 0 | Sampling | 0.2 | 0.95 | 4 | 2,048 |
|  | EvalPlus | Avg@4 | 0 | Sampling | 0.2 | 0.95 | 4 | 2,048 |
|  | MultiPL-E | Avg@4 | 0 | Sampling | 0.2 | 0.95 | 4 | 2,048 |
| Math | GSM-8K | Exact match | 0 | Greedy |  |  | 1 | 2,048 |
|  | MATH-500 | Math Verify | 0 | Greedy |  |  | 1 | 16,384 |
| Science | GPQA-Main | Exact match | 0 | Greedy |  |  | 1 | 16,384 |
|  | SuperGPQA | Exact match | 0 | Greedy |  |  | 1 | 4,096 |

Table 6: Default base-evaluation settings (except Gemma-4-26B-A4B). Rows
follow the five benchmark categories introduced in the text. $`T`$
denotes temperature, candidates are counted per problem, and generation
limits are in tokens. Greedy decoding uses $`T=0`$. MultiPL-E scores are
weighted by the number of problems in each language.

##### Scoring and aggregation.

We use exact match for the non-code benchmarks except MATH-500, whose
answers are scored with Math Verify. For HumanEval, EvalPlus, and
MultiPL-E, we report Avg@4: test-passing outcomes are averaged over the
four generated candidates for each problem and then across problems. Our
MultiPL-E evaluation covers ten languages: Python, C++, C#, Go, Java,
JavaScript, PHP, Rust, Bash, and TypeScript. We aggregate their scores
with weights proportional to the number of evaluated problems in each
language.

##### Code execution.

For HumanEval, EvalPlus, and MultiPL-E, we set the compilation and
execution timeouts to 15 seconds each. Runtime and compiler versions,
along with preparation, compilation, and execution commands, are
provided in Appendix
[D](#A4 "Appendix D Code Evaluation Environments ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")
(Table
[12](#A4.T12 "Table 12 ‣ Appendix D Code Evaluation Environments ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")).

##### Model-specific protocol selection for Gemma.

For Gemma-4-26B-A4B, limited instruction-following ability makes the
results particularly sensitive to prompting and evaluation conventions.
We therefore evaluate multiple prompt and protocol configurations and
report the maximum score obtained for each benchmark.

#### 8.1.2 Post-training Evaluation

##### General Capabilities.

We evaluate general capabilities on MMLU ([Hendrycks et al.,
2021](#bib.bib29)), MMLU-Pro ([Wang et al., 2024b](#bib.bib68)), GPQA
Diamond ([Rein et al., 2024](#bib.bib62)), AIME 2026 and HMMT February
2026 ([Balunović et al., 2025](#bib.bib10)), GSM8K ([Cobbe et al.,
2021](#bib.bib17)), MATH-500 ([Lightman et al., 2024](#bib.bib38)),
LiveCodeBench v5 and v6 ([Jain et al., 2025](#bib.bib32)), MBPP ([Austin
et al., 2021](#bib.bib8)), HumanEval ([Chen et al., 2021](#bib.bib14)),
IFBench ([Pyatkin et al., 2025](#bib.bib56)), IFEval ([Zhou et al.,
2023](#bib.bib81)), AA-LCR v1.1 ([Artificial Analysis Team,
2025](#bib.bib7)), SimpleQA Verified ([Haas et al., 2025](#bib.bib28)),
the public set of AA-Omniscience ([Jackson et al., 2025](#bib.bib31)),
CL-bench ([Dou et al., 2026b](#bib.bib20)), and CL-bench Life ([Dou et
al., 2026a](#bib.bib21)).

We use a sampling temperature of 0.6 throughout. The maximum output
length is 262,144 tokens for AIME 2026, HMMT February 2026,
LiveCodeBench v5 and v6, CL-bench, and CL-bench Life; 131,072 tokens for
GPQA Diamond; 32,768 tokens for MMLU, MMLU-Pro, GSM8K, MATH-500, MBPP,
HumanEval, IFBench, and IFEval; and 4,096 tokens for SimpleQA Verified
and AA-Omniscience. For CL-bench and CL-bench Life, top-$`p`$ is set to
0.95. We sample 32 responses per problem for AIME 2026 and HMMT February
2026; eight for LiveCodeBench v5 and v6, GPQA Diamond, MBPP, and
HumanEval; four for IFBench, IFEval, AA-LCR v1.1, CL-bench, and CL-bench
Life; and one for the remaining benchmarks.

We report accuracy for all benchmarks, averaged over the sampled
responses. Mathematical answers are graded using Math-Verify,
multiple-choice answers are compared against the reference choices, and
generated code is evaluated against the benchmark test cases. AA-LCR
v1.1 employs GPT-5.6 Luna (medium) as its judge, while SimpleQA Verified
and AA-Omniscience rely on Qwen2.5-32B as the judge. For CL-bench and
CL-bench Life, we use DeepSeek-V4.1 with thinking enabled and
rubric-level majority voting: each response is judged independently
three times, and each rubric’s verdict is determined by a majority vote.
Only final answer content is graded; responses containing only reasoning
receive zero credit on every rubric.

##### Agentic Capabilities.

We evaluate agentic capabilities on SWE-bench Verified ([Chowdhury et
al., 2024](#bib.bib47)), SWE-bench Pro ([Deng et al.,
2026](#bib.bib19)), CyberGym ([Wang et al., 2026](#bib.bib69)), and
KernelBench ([Ouyang et al., 2025](#bib.bib53)).

For SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Pro, we use the SWE-agent harness
([Yang et al., 2024](#bib.bib74)), with a sampling temperature of 0.7, a
repetition penalty of 1.1, and a maximum of 300 interaction steps. For
SWE-bench Verified, we additionally apply anti-hacking safeguards
against the shortcut behaviors summarized in Table
[4](#S6.T4 "Table 4 ‣ 6.1 Why Agentic Data Requires Agents ‣ 6 Scaling Agentic Data into Pre-Training ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?").

For KernelBench, we use a sampling temperature of 0.6, top-$`p`$ of
0.95, and a repetition penalty of 1.1. Each model turn allows up to
65,536 output tokens, with a maximum of 20 interaction rounds. Context
compression is triggered when the context reaches 150K tokens.

For CyberGym, we use the Claude Code harness ([Anthropic,
2025](#bib.bib5)), with a sampling temperature of 1.0 and top-$`p`$ of
0.95. The context window is 262,144 tokens, with automatic compression
triggered at 90% utilization. Each task attempt has a two-hour time
limit.

##### Competitive base-model performance.

801-30B-A3B achieves an average score of 73.13, the second-highest among
the seven base models, behind Qwen3.5 at 76.67 and close to
Nemotron-3.5-Lightning at 73.07. It exceeds Qwen3, Nemotron-3-Nano, and
Kimi-Linear by 6.97, 4.64, and 8.76 percentage points, respectively.
This result establishes a competitive starting point before the SFT
evaluation considered below. 801-30B-A3B obtains the highest scores on
GSM-8K and HumanEval, reaching 92.80% and 78.81%, respectively. On
MMLU-Pro, it scores 68.38%, compared with 67.01% for Qwen3.5 and 69.13%
for Nemotron-3.5-Lightning. The base-model results demonstrate a
competitive overall profile and distinct task-level strengths of our
model.

We then examine whether the strength of the base model carries over
after adaptation. Every model here is fine-tuned on the same SFT data,
which is deliberately lightweight: 6.33 B tokens and no reinforcement
learning (Section
[4.1](#S4.SS1 "4.1 Measuring Post-Training Headroom ‣ 4 Headroom Loop ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")).
Differences among the resulting models therefore mainly reflect what
each base model brings to adaptation.

Table
[8](#S8.T8 "Table 8 ‣ 8.3.1 General Capabilities ‣ 8.3 SFT Model Results ‣ 8 Evaluation ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")
reports two groups of benchmarks. The lower block contains the *classic
general benchmarks*, a suite of 13 widely used benchmarks covering the
general capabilities commonly evaluated in models of this class,
summarized by AVG13. The upper block contains five
*specialized-capability evaluations*, covering three specific areas:
long-context reasoning (AA-LCR v1.1), factual knowledge (AA-OmniScience
on its public set and SimpleQA-verified), and learning from context
(CL-bench and CL-bench Life). Their mean is reported as AVG5.

##### Performance on specialized-capability evaluations.

801-30B-A3B achieves an AVG5 of 28.70, leading Qwen3.5 (20.54) by 8.16
points and ranking first on four of the five evaluations. Its strongest
results are on long-context reasoning and factual knowledge,
particularly AA-LCR v1.1 (61.00%), AA-OmniScience (31.30%), and
SimpleQA-verified (34.50%). The pre-training corpus was decontaminated
against SimpleQA using 8-gram overlap matching, making test-set leakage
an unlikely explanation for this result. The exception is CL-bench Life,
where 801-30B-A3B trails Qwen3.5 and Nemotron-3-Nano.

##### Performance on classic general benchmarks.

801-30B-A3B achieves an AVG13 of 81.34, ranking second behind
Qwen3.5-35B-A3B (83.76), consistent with its ranking in base-model
evaluation (Table
[7](#S8.T7 "Table 7 ‣ 8.2 Base Model Evaluation ‣ 8 Evaluation ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")).
It performs particularly well on mathematics and code, matching the
highest Math500 score (98.40%) and reaching 95.75% on GSM8K and 95.12%
on HumanEval. Its main weaknesses are in competitive programming and
instruction following, as reflected by its results on LiveCodeBench v5
and IFEval Strict.

### 8.4 Learning aptitude

Figure 25: Learning aptitude of 801-30B-A3B and Qwen3-30B-A3B on
SWE-bench Pro (left) and BFCL Full (right). Hollow markers are scores at
successive SFT checkpoints; the pale line is the least-squares fit of
Eq.
([1](#S4.E1 "In 4.1 Measuring Post-Training Headroom ‣ 4 Headroom Loop ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")),
and $`k`$ in the legend is its slope, the gain in points per tenfold
increase in SFT steps.

##### Lower start, faster learning on BFCL

At the first checkpoint (step 55), 801-30B-A3B scores 31.32 on BFCL
Full, below the 40.04 of Qwen3-30B-A3B. Its slope, however, is 8.62
points per tenfold increase in SFT steps against 3.33, about
$`2.6\times`$ steeper. From step 697 onward it leads at every shared
checkpoint and ends at 48.65 against 46.26 at step 3,485. This is the
case that motivates learning aptitude: a checkpoint that starts lower
but learns faster overtakes one that starts higher once fine-tuning runs
long enough.

##### Higher start and faster learning on SWE-bench Pro

On SWE-bench Pro, 801-30B-A3B leads from the first checkpoint, 26.95
against 0 at step 30, and learns faster, with a slope of 9.15 against
5.03. Qwen3-30B-A3B stays at zero for the first three checkpoints (up to
step 120) and reaches 8.76 at step 1,922, where 801-30B-A3B reaches
43.37. Here the intercept and the slope point the same way, so the gap
widens rather than closes as fine-tuning continues.

## 9 Conclusion

We attempted to answer a question that current RSI successes leave open:
what can agents do for frontier pre-training, where the
$`\textit{propose}\rightarrow\textit{run}\rightarrow\textit{measure}\rightarrow\textit{update}`$
loop cannot close because the run is not repeatable and the objective is
not a score? Our answer, drawn from building 801-30B-A3B in three
months, is to organize improvement around three types of loops.
Debugging loops comprise the infra debugging loop and the data debugging
loop, which connect unusual internal metrics and output patterns to
their causes. Five cross-stack diagnoses, resolved in about one month,
came out of these investigations. The headroom loop is instantiated as
the recipe loop, using tiny-SFT, learning aptitude, and
max-over-protocols evaluation to guide recipe revisions and monitor
training progress. Experience-to-metric loops comprise the classifier
development loop, the site discovery loop, and the crawl-coverage loop,
turning experience-based judgment into feedback that agents can use to
improve data workflows. All of them share a context infrastructure that
integrates evidence across teams at scale and preserves negative results
and their reasons.

The resulting model is evidence that this regime works at scale.
801-30B-A3B is state-of-the-art among open base models at the 30B MoE
scale in both direct base evaluation and matched-SFT comparison, and
after a 6B-token SFT stage it approaches a fully post-trained frontier
of its size class on agentic tasks. But we hold the model to be the
byproduct and the account to be the contribution. Our experience
suggests that RSI need not stop at frontier pre-training. It takes a
different form: loops eliminate anomalies, headroom measurements guide
training, and quantitative feedback improves data workflows. Shared
context allows evidence and lessons to accumulate across teams and
iterations. There may be no second run, but the one we have can still
learn from its own progress.

## Appendix A Layer-wise MaxVio Monitoring

Figure
[26](#A1.F26 "Figure 26 ‣ Appendix A Layer-wise MaxVio Monitoring ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")
reports the MaxVio trajectories for all 48 Mixture-of-Experts layers
over training. Most layers remain within a relatively stable range,
while a small number develop substantially larger violations; in
particular, layer 15 exhibits the pronounced rise discussed in Figure
[7](#S3.F7 "Figure 7 ‣ 3.1 Infra Debugging Loop ‣ 3 Debugging Loops ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?").
The vertical dashed lines indicate the stage boundaries, and the
horizontal axis is training tokens in trillions.

## Appendix C Evaluation Protocols for Base Models

Figure
[13](#S4.F13 "Figure 13 ‣ 4.1 Measuring Post-Training Headroom ‣ 4 Headroom Loop ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")
evaluates the same checkpoints under several protocols. A protocol is
determined by four choices: perplexity-based (PPL) or generation-based
scoring, the number of in-context examples (k-shot), the required
final-answer format, and the answer-matching method. Table
[11](#A3.T11 "Table 11 ‣ Appendix C Evaluation Protocols for Base Models ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?")
defines each protocol label used in the figure.

|  |  |  |  |
|----|----|----|----|
|  Protocol |  In-context examples |  Final-answer format |  Scoring |
| Non-code tasks |  |  |  |
|  5-shot |  5 solved examples: final answers only for ARC, GPQA-Main, MMLU-Redux, and AGIEval-EN; worked solutions for MMLU-Pro and SuperGPQA |  “The answer is (X).”, shown by the examples |  Extracted letter, exact match |
|  4-shot Minerva |  4 worked solutions in Minerva format (MATH-500) |  Follows the examples |  Math equivalence |
|  8-shot CoT |  8 worked solutions (GSM-8K) |  “The answer is N.” |  Strict match, exact match |
|  3-shot CoT |  3 official worked solutions per subtask (BBH) |  “the answer is …” |  Extracted answer, exact match |
|  0-shot answer-is |  None |  Instructed to end with “the answer is X” |  Extracted answer, exact match^(†) |
|  0-shot boxed |  None |  Instructed to put the answer in \boxed{} |  Extracted answer, exact match^(†) |
|  PPL acc_norm |  None |  No generation |  Highest length-normalized option log-likelihood |
| Code tasks |  |  |  |
|  3-shot completion |  3 |  Continue the bare function signature and docstring |  Unit tests, pass@1 |
|  k-shot instruction + signature |  3 or 0 |  Instruction prompt; signature pre-filled in the answer |  Unit tests, pass@1 |
|  k-shot instruction, no signature |  3 or 0 |  Instruction prompt; the model writes the full function |  Unit tests, pass@1 |

^(†)Math equivalence for MATH-500.

Table 11: Evaluation protocols in Figure
[13](#S4.F13 "Figure 13 ‣ 4.1 Measuring Post-Training Headroom ‣ 4 Headroom Loop ‣ No Second Run: Does RSI Stop at Frontier Pre-training?").
````
